opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I try to avoid framing things around a single threshold called "AGI," because I think that concept bundles together a lot of capabilities that don't necessarily arrive together and don't necessarily matter in the same ways. It suggests there's one axis of "general intelligence," that we're moving along it, and that at some point we cross a line and everything changes. I don't think that's a very accurate picture of either human or machine intelligence.

So instead I'd frame forecasts in terms of specific capabilities and the societal functions they could affect. Can systems reliably carry out long-horizon tasks in open-ended environments? Can they do scientific research end to end, or only pieces of it? Can they model what other people want and coordinate with them, or do they just follow instructions in a narrow sense? Those are different questions, and progress on one doesn't straightforwardly imply progress on the others. You can have systems that are superhuman at writing code or at certain kinds of math while still being quite brittle at grounded, embodied reasoning, or at understanding the norms of a particular community.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that the impact of AI isn't just a function of capability. It depends on deployment: who has access, which institutions adopt it, how much autonomy and authority we delegate to these systems, and what kinds of oversight exist. Two worlds with the same underlying technical capabilities could look very different depending on those choices. So when I think about forecasting, I'd rather ask "what tasks could be automated, at what reliability and cost, and in which domains would that be transformative or destabilizing?" than "when will AGI arrive?"

That framing is also more actionable. If you think of AGI as a single event, policy tends to collapse into a race-or-pause debate. If you think in terms of specific capabilities and deployment contexts, you can target interventions: evaluations for particular dangerous capabilities, norms for when systems can act autonomously, and institutional design that keeps humans meaningfully in the loop where it matters. And it leaves room for something I care about a lot: thinking about what kinds of AI systems we actually want to build, systems that are helpful and cooperative within human social contexts, rather than treating some maximally general, maximally autonomous agent as the inevitable endpoint.

r001.rationale: It proposes forecasting by specific capabilities, tasks, and deployment contexts, but does not frame forecasts around automating a substantial fraction of the existing industrial economy.

r002.rationale: It says deployment depends on access, institutional adoption, delegated authority, and oversight, but does not state that regulatory or societal constraints can prevent technically feasible AI automation from being deployed.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate for when automation of 50–80% of the existing industrial economy might be technically feasible.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss large AI companies’ forecasts or how their definitions of AGI shape those forecasts.

r005.rationale: It does not assess whether large AI companies’ forecasts are too optimistic under their own definitions of AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that I try not to forecast "AGI" at all, because I think the term bundles together a bunch of things that don't have to arrive together, and once you unbundle them the question gets much more tractable.

When people say "when will we get AGI," they're usually imagining a single threshold: a system that can do essentially any cognitive task a human can do, at human level or better. But intelligence isn't one-dimensional, and the tasks we care about aren't drawn from a single distribution. So I'd rather ask about specific capabilities in specific domains, under specific conditions. Can a system autonomously run a multi-week software project? Can it conduct original scientific research where the feedback loop is slow and expensive? Can it operate in the physical world with the reliability we'd demand from a human worker? Those are different questions with different answers and different timelines, and I think the "AGI" framing actively obscures that by implying they'll all flip at once.

The second thing I'd say is that I try to separate capability from deployment and from impact. A lot of the forecasts that get the most attention are really forecasts about benchmark performance, and benchmarks are, by construction, the tasks we know how to specify cleanly and verify cheaply. That's a biased sample of what matters. So when I see a trend line on some eval, I ask: what's the gap between doing well on this and doing the actual job? Often it's about robustness, about handling the long tail, about knowing when you don't know. Those are the things that are hard to put on a chart, and they're exactly the things that determine whether the economic or societal impact shows up.

And then there's the question of what we even mean by "general." Humans aren't general-purpose reasoners either. We're very good at a particular set of things because of our evolutionary history and our cultural scaffolding, and we're embarrassingly bad at others. So "human-level" is a moving and somewhat arbitrary target. I think a more useful framing is to ask what kinds of problems a system can solve, with what kind of supervision, at what cost, and how that's changing over time.

So if you push me for a forecast, I'll give you one, but it'll be in the form of "I expect systems to be able to do X reliably within Y years, conditional on Z," rather than a date for some singular event. I think that's more honest, more falsifiable, and frankly more useful for anyone who actually has to make decisions about this stuff, whether that's policy or safety research or just deciding what to work on.

r001.rationale: It recommends forecasting specific capabilities by domain and conditions, but does not frame forecasts around automating a substantial fraction of the existing industrial economy.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes capability from deployment and impact, but does not state that regulatory or societal constraints can prevent technically feasible automation from being deployed.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate for automating 50–80% of the existing industrial economy.

r004.rationale: It critiques the AGI framing generally, but says nothing about large AI companies’ forecasts or how their definitions of AGI affect them.

r005.rationale: It does not assess large AI companies’ forecasts or judge them too optimistic under their own AGI definitions.

astra-6.text:
I tend to prefer talking about particular capabilities and the conditions under which we expect them to emerge. What kinds of tasks can a system do? How reliably can it do them? How much human supervision does it need? Those seem like more useful forecasting questions than asking when we’ll get AGI, because people mean quite different things by that term.

My reservation is that “general intelligence” sounds like a single property that you either have or don’t have. But intelligence involves many different capacities, and progress across those capacities can be uneven. A system might be extremely strong in one domain and still struggle with something that seems quite straightforward to a human.

So I’d rather make forecasts that are conditional and specific: if we continue with these approaches, with these resources, what abilities should we expect, and where might the limitations remain? You can still make consequential predictions about AI without treating AGI as a single finish line.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to prefer thinking about specific capabilities and the conditions under which they emerge, rather than forecasting a single moment when we achieve AGI. What kinds of tasks can a system do? How reliably can it do them? How much human assistance does it need, and how well does it adapt when the environment changes? Those are more concrete questions, and people can disagree about the answers without also disagreeing about what intelligence means.

I also think we need to distinguish capabilities from deployment and impact. A system might perform well on a benchmark, but that doesn’t immediately tell us whether it can replace someone’s work or function autonomously over long periods. So I’d rather make conditional forecasts about particular abilities and applications, with explicit assumptions and uncertainty, than put a date on a category whose boundaries aren’t very clear.
